raw_graphql_pull_request.body:
﻿## Overview

Fix probabilistic rejection sampling when the draft vocabulary is narrower than the target vocabulary in both Model Runner V1 and V2, including the CPU V1 fallback.

Fixes #61112.
Fixes #61113.

## Claims

- Treat q(token) as zero for target-only token IDs without materializing padded draft tensors.
- Prevent V1 GPU and CPU kernels from reading narrow draft-probability rows with the target row width.
- Keep the CPU override, C++ signatures, and Torch operator schemas aligned with the V1 dispatch arguments.
- Preserve the full target vocabulary in V2 ordinary, block, and watermarked recovery.
- Keep equal-width, one-hot, greedy, and synthetic verification behavior unchanged.

## Validation

### CUDA

Hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050, 8 GB; Torch 2.13.0+cu130; Python 3.12.

Command: `python -m pytest -q tests/v1/sample/test_rejection_sampler.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_rejection_sampler_utils.py`

Result: **137 passed**.

The narrow-vocabulary V2 regression is parameterized over standard and block verification. The watermarked path has separate coverage.

Independent 50,000-request CUDA evaluations used target probabilities `[0.5, 0.3, 0.2]` and narrower draft probabilities `[0.3, 0.7]`:

| Runner | Observed first-token frequencies |
|---|---|
| V1 | `[0.4976, 0.3003, 0.2021]` |
| V2 | `[0.5001, 0.2991, 0.2008]` |

Both recover the target-only token and match the target distribution within the predeclared 0.015 absolute tolerance.

### CPU

Built the editable CPU extension under WSL with Python 3.12 and Torch 2.13.0+cpu, including the `_C`, `_C_AVX2`, and `_C_AVX512` variants.

For the dispatch-order follow-up, Triton was removed from the isolated CPU environment and `HAS_TRITON=False` was confirmed before running:

Command: `python -m pytest -q tests/v1/e2e/test_cpu_spec_decode.py::test_cpu_rejection_sampler_supports_narrow_draft_probs`

Result: **1 passed**.

The regression launches both kernels through `KernelOverride` using the original Triton argument names, then executes the genuine CPU C++ fallback. It covers positional forwarding, residual recovery of a target-only token, and acceptance handling of a draft token ID outside the draft probability width. Static signature validation also confirms that both CPU override orders exactly match their Triton kernels.

### Static checks

Command: `pre-commit run --files csrc/cpu/spec_decode_utils.cpp csrc/cpu/torch_bindings.cpp vllm/utils/cpu_triton_utils.py tests/v1/e2e/test_cpu_spec_decode.py`

All applicable hooks passed, including ruff, formatting, clang-format, mypy, test tethering, SPDX, forbidden imports, CUDA API checks, Docker graph validation, suggestions, and DCO sign-off.

A representative review microcheck showed that padding a 128 x 5 x 66 BF16 V2 buffer to width 50,257 allocated 61.3 MiB and cost about 1.67 ms per call. The final implementation performs masked in-kernel loads and introduces no padded allocation.

## Details

The V1 kernels used the target vocabulary width as the draft row stride and residual-loop bound. Narrow draft tensors therefore caused cross-row and out-of-bounds reads. The fix passes the real draft stride and width to the acceptance and recovery kernels and returns zero for out-of-range draft probabilities.

The CPU override and C++ Torch operator schemas now accept the same dispatch arguments. The C++ acceptance path treats an out-of-range draft token as having zero draft probability, while the residual loop reads draft probabilities only below `draft_vocab_size`.

V2 previously truncated the target vocabulary to the draft width. The first patch corrected the distribution by padding the full max-capacity draft-logit buffer on every verification call, but that introduced substantial steady-state allocation and copy overhead. The final fix instead threads the draft width through the logits-statistics, acceptance, block-verification, residual, and resampling kernels and masks draft loads beyond that width to negative infinity.

The change adds no host reads, device synchronization, public API, or documentation requirement. Model Runner V1 is included because #61113 demonstrates incorrect and potentially out-of-bounds behavior on deployments that still require that runner; Model Runner V2 is independently affected by #61112.

This does not duplicate #42775. That PR adds opt-in model-loading and output masking for suffix-compatible `draft_model` pairs. This PR repairs rejection sampling for already-produced narrow probabilistic tensors, including EAGLE-style heads, in both runner implementations.

AI assistance was used to review and refine this change. The human submitter reviewed every changed line, ran the listed CUDA and CPU tests, and is responsible for the implementation.

---

- [x] I used vLLM's `/pr-checklist` skill.
- [x] AI assistance was used during the creation of this PR.

- [x] **Design Fit:** Minimizes impact on core components, reuses existing functionality, and justifies added complexity.
- [x] **Testing and Validation:** Validates the change and ensures added tests are meaningful and reliable, with CI coverage and documented local validation.
- [x] **Code Quality and Style:** Keeps code and comments clear and concise; no user-facing documentation changes are required.
- [x] **Pull Request Contents:** Includes a brief summary and relevant links, supports claims with evidence, explains root causes and implementation trade-offs, and follows the contributing guide.
</details>

nodes.body: Hey @SeverinVisionary could you rerun the original macOS C++ and triton-cpu reproducers, plus the narrow EAGLE end-to-end case if feasible? I only have CUDA hardware.

Thanks @maithilijoshi20. I reran the original N7 C++ reproducer on Linux x86-64, with `--device cpu --batches 20`, using separate CPU builds of `bfa7e5b7a` and `5a79873df`. Both used Torch 2.13.0+cpu and the genuine C++ fallback (`HAS_TRITON=False`).

On the parent, the padded control emitted 0/9,898 tokens outside the target support; the narrow and narrow_m1 cases each emitted 3,345/9,898. On the PR head, the first padded-control call failed before returning a result:

```text
RuntimeError: _C::sample_recovered_tokens_kernel_impl() Expected a value of type 'Tensor' for argument 'target_probs' but instead found type 'int'.
Position: 4
Value: 50257
```

This looks like an argument-order mismatch in the CPU override. `sample_recovered_tokens_kernel` puts `draft_probs_stride` immediately after `draft_probs`, while `_sample_recovered_tokens_kernel_impl` puts it after `vocab_size`. `KernelOverride._launch` forwards in the original kernel's order, so the padded stride, 50257, reaches `target_probs`. The same ordering difference appears in the random-rejection CPU override too.

I kept that first failure without patching or rerunning the arm. The remaining fix cases, triton-cpu and EAGLE checks did not run, so I can't confirm the full fix yet. macOS remains untested.

AI assistance was used for the retest, evidence review and this write-up.

Thanks, @SeverinVisionary. The CPU override argument ordering is fixed, and the regression now launches through KernelOverride before reaching the genuine C++ fallback. Locally, it passes with HAS_TRITON=False.
If possible, could you rerun the original N7 C++ reproducer with --device cpu --batches 20 against the current head?

Thanks @maithilijoshi20. I reran the unchanged original N7 reproducer with `--device cpu --batches 20` at `63184b36e8830e2b67b215313047e1e797a24fa2`.

On Linux x86_64 with Torch 2.13.0+cpu, genuine `HAS_TRITON=False` and the production `KernelOverride`/C++ path, it exited 0. The padded argument-type error from my earlier run at `5a79873` did not recur. All three cases—`padded`, `narrow` and `narrow_m1`—reported 0/9,898 off-support emitted tokens. Each case printed rounded first-token frequencies `a=.504, b=.286, c=.210, other=0`, against the toy target law `.5/.3/.2`. These finite observations do not establish statistical exactness or token-for-token equality between cases.

This used the exact new Python source with the retained source-built native libraries from `5a79873`. I checked the complete direct source-tree comparison: only the CPU Python adapter and regression test changed; the native/build inputs and operator ABI are unchanged. This is a component retest, rather than a fresh full-head distribution build.

I also attempted `test_cpu_rejection_sampler_supports_narrow_draft_probs` once. Pytest stopped while importing `tests/conftest.py` because `tblib` is missing: zero tests collected or executed. macOS/ARM, genuine triton-cpu V1/V2, EAGLE and engine/model generation remain untested in this follow-up.

AI assistance was used for the retest, evidence review and this write-up.

## Claude Code Review

This pull request is from a fork — automated review is disabled. A repository maintainer can comment `@claude review` to run a one-time review.

issue_comments.body: Hey @SeverinVisionary could you rerun the original macOS C++ and triton-cpu reproducers, plus the narrow EAGLE end-to-end case if feasible? I only have CUDA hardware.

Thanks @maithilijoshi20. I reran the original N7 C++ reproducer on Linux x86-64, with `--device cpu --batches 20`, using separate CPU builds of `bfa7e5b7a` and `5a79873df`. Both used Torch 2.13.0+cpu and the genuine C++ fallback (`HAS_TRITON=False`).

On the parent, the padded control emitted 0/9,898 tokens outside the target support; the narrow and narrow_m1 cases each emitted 3,345/9,898. On the PR head, the first padded-control call failed before returning a result:

```text
RuntimeError: _C::sample_recovered_tokens_kernel_impl() Expected a value of type 'Tensor' for argument 'target_probs' but instead found type 'int'.
Position: 4
Value: 50257
```

This looks like an argument-order mismatch in the CPU override. `sample_recovered_tokens_kernel` puts `draft_probs_stride` immediately after `draft_probs`, while `_sample_recovered_tokens_kernel_impl` puts it after `vocab_size`. `KernelOverride._launch` forwards in the original kernel's order, so the padded stride, 50257, reaches `target_probs`. The same ordering difference appears in the random-rejection CPU override too.

I kept that first failure without patching or rerunning the arm. The remaining fix cases, triton-cpu and EAGLE checks did not run, so I can't confirm the full fix yet. macOS remains untested.

AI assistance was used for the retest, evidence review and this write-up.

Thanks, @SeverinVisionary. The CPU override argument ordering is fixed, and the regression now launches through KernelOverride before reaching the genuine C++ fallback. Locally, it passes with HAS_TRITON=False.
If possible, could you rerun the original N7 C++ reproducer with --device cpu --batches 20 against the current head?

Thanks @maithilijoshi20. I reran the unchanged original N7 reproducer with `--device cpu --batches 20` at `63184b36e8830e2b67b215313047e1e797a24fa2`.

On Linux x86_64 with Torch 2.13.0+cpu, genuine `HAS_TRITON=False` and the production `KernelOverride`/C++ path, it exited 0. The padded argument-type error from my earlier run at `5a79873` did not recur. All three cases—`padded`, `narrow` and `narrow_m1`—reported 0/9,898 off-support emitted tokens. Each case printed rounded first-token frequencies `a=.504, b=.286, c=.210, other=0`, against the toy target law `.5/.3/.2`. These finite observations do not establish statistical exactness or token-for-token equality between cases.

This used the exact new Python source with the retained source-built native libraries from `5a79873`. I checked the complete direct source-tree comparison: only the CPU Python adapter and regression test changed; the native/build inputs and operator ABI are unchanged. This is a component retest, rather than a fresh full-head distribution build.

I also attempted `test_cpu_rejection_sampler_supports_narrow_draft_probs` once. Pytest stopped while importing `tests/conftest.py` because `tblib` is missing: zero tests collected or executed. macOS/ARM, genuine triton-cpu V1/V2, EAGLE and engine/model generation remain untested in this follow-up.

AI assistance was used for the retest, evidence review and this write-up.
